title: Local business retention depends more on relational ecosystem and usable support than on headline cost ratings alone
source_unit: Gallup Pathways to Wealth, Half of U.S. Business Owners See Local Area as Good for Business, September 8, 2026
geography: United States; business owners, primarily recruited from the probability-based Gallup Panel

denominator.unit: Gallup Pathways to Wealth Year 3 business-owner survey; public article does not disclose the respondent count

positive_local_view.unit: percent holding a positive view of their city or local area as a place to run a business

negative_local_view.unit: percent holding a negative overall view

neutral_local_view.unit: percent neutral about the local area

likely_to_leave_overall.unit: percent likely to leave their current area within 12 months for a business-related reason

observations.method: Gallup Pathways to Wealth Year 3 survey conducted September 26-November 3, 2025, with business owners recruited primarily from the probability-based Gallup Panel; publication released September 2026.
observations.uncertainty: The public article does not report the business-owner sample size, full weighting details, sector composition or exact analytic denominators; satisfaction and relocation intention are self-reported and not observed moves or firm exits.
observations.subgroup: U.S. business owners, with comparisons by overall local-climate view and expected revenue growth.
observations.counterinterpretation: Owners may rate a place through the lens of their own firm performance, and positive local sentiment may reflect selection into places already favorable to their business rather than local conditions causing success.

observations.period: September 26-November 3, 2025 survey; local cost and market conditions

denominator.unit: Gallup business-owner survey; public article does not disclose the respondent count

real_estate_deterrent.unit: percent agreeing commercial and residential real estate costs deter business development

taxes_too_high.unit: percent agreeing state and local tax rates are too high to support business growth

access_to_customers.unit: percent agreeing their area provides good access to customers and markets

business_to_business_support.unit: percent agreeing their area provides helpful business-to-business support services

professional_suppliers.unit: percent agreeing their area offers good access to professional service suppliers

observations.method: Business owners rated 11 local business-climate conditions; the publication compares item prevalence with overall satisfaction and relocation intentions.
observations.uncertainty: Item agreement does not measure actual prices, tax incidence, network use, customer volume or service quality; the study does not establish causal rankings among local conditions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. business owners across local markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: High cost ratings may be salient but not decisive: owners may tolerate costs when customer access, networks, regulation and public services make the business viable.

observations.period: September 26-November 3, 2025 survey; dissatisfaction and relocation intention

denominator.unit: Gallup business-owner survey; subgroup sample sizes not disclosed in the public article

negative_view_likely_to_leave.unit: percent of owners with a negative overall local-climate view likely to leave within 12 months for a business reason

nonnegative_view_likely_to_leave.unit: percent among owners without a negative overall view

relocation_difference.unit: percentage-point descriptive difference in relocation intention

retention_mechanism.value: Local dissatisfaction is associated with owner exit intention, but the association is stronger where business growth raises the value of finding a better ecosystem.

observations.method: Gallup comparison of self-reported likelihood of leaving the local area within 12 months by overall business-climate satisfaction.
observations.uncertainty: The relationship is correlational and could reflect firm performance, owner mobility, sector composition, local shocks or unmeasured opportunity differences; stated intention is not relocation.
observations.subgroup: Business owners with negative versus neutral or positive local-climate views.
observations.counterinterpretation: Owners considering relocation may retrospectively rate the local climate negatively, so intention can shape satisfaction rather than only result from it.

observations.period: September 26-November 3, 2025 survey; growth expectations and local dissatisfaction

denominator.unit: Gallup business-owner survey; subgroup sample sizes not disclosed in the public article

growth_and_dissatisfied_likely_to_leave.unit: percent of owners expecting annual revenue growth and dissatisfied with the local area who were likely to relocate

growth_and_satisfied_or_neutral_likely_t.unit: percent of owners expecting growth but satisfied or neutral about the local area

nongrowth_and_dissatisfied_likely_to_lea.unit: percent of owners not expecting growth and dissatisfied with the local area

growth_mobility_interaction.unit: percentage-point descriptive difference between growth-expecting dissatisfied owners and growth-expecting satisfied or neutral owners

observations.method: Gallup cross-tabulation of local-climate satisfaction, expected revenue growth and relocation intention.
observations.uncertainty: The interaction is descriptive, uses expectations rather than verified revenue, and does not show whether relocation would improve firm outcomes or local economic stability.
observations.subgroup: Business owners by expected revenue growth and local-climate satisfaction.
observations.counterinterpretation: Growth-oriented owners may have more mobility options and higher standards, making the same local friction more consequential than for firms prioritizing stability or survival.

boundary: This record adds a place-and-firm retention mechanism: local business ecosystems are judged through customer access, support networks, regulation and public services, while dissatisfaction is associated with owner relocation intention, especially among growth-expecting firms. It does not establish causal local-policy effects, actual moves, firm survival, employment, revenue, tax base or community welfare outcomes.
